source.title: Spelling Bee Embeddings for Language Modeling
source.authors: Markus Rabe; J. Clymo; Zhe Dong

record.tranche_reason: The study conducts a language-model scaling sweep and measures held-out test loss, but uses its own spelling-embedding comparison and a fixed parameter-to-token ratio rather than reproducing the original scaling-law analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a shifted-power-law fit to its test-loss scaling sweep and describes the aggregate trend in text, but does not give the fit coefficients or individual plotted values. The 816m benchmark table compares scores at one scale; it does not test downstream predictability with scale or pretraining loss. Spelling-task results likewise do not test these scaling versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses scaling-law methods as a tool to compare its spelling bee embeddings with a baseline. It fits shifted power laws to its 44m–816m runs to express a compute advantage of about 8%. It does not assess whether loss follows a power law, report fit quality or exponents, test extrapolation, or sweep allocations. The 20:1 ratio check is a one-sentence remark with no data.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that the embeddings improve most lm-evaluation-harness benchmarks and spelling tasks (count +14.8%, index +5.9%, reverse 0%). They also find the advantage does not diminish with 10× Chinchilla data. They frame the results as an architecture improvement, not as evidence about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a new embedding modification with a baseline and fits shifted power laws over model sizes; it keeps a 20:1 token-to-parameter ratio rather than reproducing the original scaling-law or compute-optimal allocation analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss advantage is compared across model sizes and is described as relatively constant over two orders of magnitude of compute. The 106m data-saturation comparison varies training data from 1× to 10× Chinchilla.

fits_no_version.finding: Spelling bee embeddings give a loss advantage equivalent to about 8% more FLOPs, roughly constant across two orders of magnitude of compute (44m–816m). At 106m the compute advantage is 9.8% at 1× and 12.5% at 10× Chinchilla data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from embedding-level architecture changes persist (do not shrink) with model scale and training data.

record.problems: The scaling study reaches about 800m parameters and uses a single stated training dataset. The text gives no scaling-fit coefficients or uncertainty estimates, and the data-amount comparison has only two points. The authors note that benefits may disappear at larger scale or with different datasets or vocabularies.
record.rows_left_out: The single-configuration benchmark comparisons in Table 2 and spelling-task results in Tables 3 and Sections 5.1–5.2 do not test scaling predictability or the compute-optimal allocation versions, so they were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Power-law form of loss in parameters, tokens or compute is assumed for fitting, not evaluated; no fit quality or exponents are reported.
No extrapolation from small to larger runs is tested.
No allocation sweep across compute budgets; the 20:1 check is unreported.
No controlled shape comparison at fixed parameters.
Benchmarks are reported at one scale only (Table 2).
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: The data behind the 20:1 ratio validation (budgets, ratios tried, losses) is not reported anywhere in the text, so it cannot be recorded.

record.verdict_notes: This is an architecture paper. The shifted power-law fits in Figure 3 are a measurement tool for the compute advantage. The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V1/V3 labels are therefore removed. Table 5 ablations and the Appendix C SwiGLU reproduction are also method comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: The parameter and compute sweep varies model size with a fixed 20:1 token-to-parameter ratio, so it does not isolate parameter, token, and compute scaling. The separate data comparison covers only 1× and 10× Chinchilla data, not several orders of magnitude.
No test of whether fits to small runs predict substantially larger runs is reported.

The study says a 20:1 token-to-parameter ratio was roughly optimal for its base model and dataset, but does not report an allocation sweep across compute budgets or test how parameter and token counts grow with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Only text pretraining is studied; other modalities, repeated-data regimes beyond the stated comparison, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
Benchmark results are reported at one model configuration, without testing whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The paper uses shifted-power-law fits but does not compare fitting choices or exponents, test disagreements between published laws, or report a curve bending away from a single law.

rows.subject: 44m–816m model scaling runs (aggregate; baseline and spelling bee variants)
rows.size_stated: 44m–816m configurations; actual parameter counts vary from the configuration names
rows.operation_detail: Scale model size and training compute; fit shifted power laws to SlimPajama test loss.

conditions.value: Transformer baseline vs spelling bee embeddings

rows.value: Spelling bee embeddings improve test loss; the fitted curves indicate about 8% more FLOPs for the same test loss, with the advantage relatively constant across two orders of magnitude of compute.
rows.note: Aggregate result as described by the authors; the figure's individual points and fit coefficients are not stated in the text.
rows.check: This row compares the study's own method with a baseline (an 8% FLOP advantage). Neither the text nor the figure description assesses whether the power-law form holds. No fit coefficients, residuals or plotted values are given.

rows.subject: 106m Transformer baseline
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss at the 1× Chinchilla training-data amount.
rows.note: The 1× point is reported separately; the token-scaling trend is assessed by comparison with the 10× point.
rows.check: A single loss point at 1× Chinchilla data, used for the embedding comparison. It cannot show any scaling form.

rows.subject: 106m Transformer with spelling bee embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Measure test loss at the 1× Chinchilla training-data amount.
rows.note: The 1× point is reported separately; the token-scaling trend is assessed by comparison with the 10× point.
rows.check: A single loss point for the study's own method variant. It is a method comparison, not a scaling test.

rows.subject: 106m Transformer baseline
rows.operation_detail: Increase training data from 1× to 10× the Chinchilla amount.
rows.note: Only two data amounts are reported; this result does not establish a power law over several orders of magnitude.
rows.check: There are only two data amounts (1× and 10×). Lower loss with 10× more data cannot distinguish a power law from other forms. The experiment tests whether the embedding advantage persists.

rows.subject: 106m Transformer with spelling bee embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Increase training data from 1× to 10× the Chinchilla amount.
rows.note: Only two data amounts are reported; this result does not establish a power law over several orders of magnitude.
rows.check: Same as R4: two points for the method variant, a method comparison rather than a scaling test.

rows.subject: Base model (size not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Validate the adopted token-to-parameter training ratio as roughly optimal for the base model.
rows.value: The 20:1 ratio was roughly optimal for the base model and SlimPajama dataset.
rows.note: This is a reported validation for one base-model setup, not a trend across compute budgets.
rows.check: It is an unquantified one-sentence claim that 20:1 was 'roughly optimal' on the base model. No budgets, ratios tested or losses are reported, and it covers one budget, so it cannot show how allocation grows with compute.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
